q: What should you settle before you open any data?
options: The decision the number will support
How many rows the table has
why: A number with no decision attached is trivia. Start from what someone will do differently because of the answer.

q: Net margin is computed as total profit divided by total revenue, not as the average of each entity's margin. Why?
options: Averaging percentages gives a tiny entity the same weight as a huge one
why: Ratios are non-additive. Add the numerators and denominators first, then divide: that weights every dollar equally.

q: One day shows $0 revenue, a cost, and the status 'Cancelled'. What is the best first move?
options: Delete it so it doesn't drag the averages
Replace the zero with the average revenue
Find out whether it is a real cancellation before deciding to keep or exclude it
Ignore it, it is only one row
why: Never fix what you haven't understood. A genuine cancellation is information; a broken import is a defect.

q: You want to show how three categories share total revenue. Which chart fits best?
options: A scatter plot of category names
A line chart over the category names
A sorted bar chart or a simple donut of share of total
why: Share of a whole needs a part-to-whole view with few, labelled slices. Sorting makes the comparison readable.

q: What makes a KPI more than a vanity metric?
options: It is displayed in large type
It has a target, a direction, and someone who acts when it turns red
why: A KPI exists to trigger a decision. Without a target and an owner it is just a number.

q: In DAX, a measure is CALCULATE([Total Sales], Sales[Country] = "USA"). In a table grouped by Country, what does the Germany row show?
options: Zero, because Germany is not USA
The USA total, because the filter replaces the row's Country filter
why: CALCULATE overrides the filter on the same column, so every row shows the USA figure. To keep the row context you would filter a different column or use KEEPFILTERS.

q: A budget line is revenue: budget 100,000, actual 112,000. A cost line: budget 40,000, actual 47,000. Which is favourable?
why: Above budget is good for revenue and bad for a cost. Variance is actual minus budget, and 'favourable' depends on the line's kind.

q: A series rises by 2,000 every month. Why does a 3-month moving average forecast badly?
options: It averages the past, so it lags a steady trend instead of extending it
Moving averages only work on seasonal data
It is always the most accurate method
why: An average of recent values sits behind the latest point. A trend method such as Holt or a linear fit extends the slope.

q: OCR reads an invoice. Subtotal 459.98, tax 36.80, total 469.78. What is the right next step?
options: Post it, the OCR is usually right
Flag it: 459.98 + 36.80 is 496.78, so a digit was probably transposed
why: Arithmetic checks catch OCR slips. Never edit one number to make the sum work without looking at the original.

q: You join orders to order lines on order_id and total revenue doubles. What is the most likely cause?
options: The join key repeats on one side, so values are counted more than once
why: A one-to-many join repeats the 'one' side's values for every matching row, so summing afterwards counts them again. Check the key is unique on the side you expect before joining.

q: Before running an UPDATE that cleans a column, what should you do first?
options: Run it and look at the result afterwards
Run a SELECT with the same WHERE to see which rows would change, ideally on a copy
Delete the column and re-create it
why: A SELECT with the same condition shows exactly what the UPDATE would touch. Doing it on a copy means a mistake costs nothing.

q: What is the 'grain' of a table?
options: The number of rows it has
The data type of its key
The order it is sorted in
why: Grain is the meaning of one row (one sale, one customer per day). Every join and every sum depends on knowing it.

q: A KPI is below target. What is the most useful next query?
options: Select every row and read them
Break the KPI down by the dimensions that could explain it (entity, category, period) and compare to target
Delete the rows with the worst values
Re-run the KPI with a different formula
why: A breakdown shows where the gap comes from. That turns 'the number is off' into 'these two entities explain it'.

q: Which of these is a finding rather than just an observation?
options: The chart shows cost by entity
Cost is 12% over budget, driven by two entities; review their spend next quarter
why: A finding is a claim, the evidence for it and a 'so what'. The first two are only observations.

q: How do you know a report is ready to deliver?
options: It contains every table you made
A person who was not in the room could act on it
It is longer than one page
why: A report exists to change a decision. If someone outside the room cannot act on it, it is not finished. Keep the caveats, they help the reader judge the numbers.

q: A subgroup of 30 people shows 44%. Compared with a subgroup of 40 showing 16%, you should...
options: Test the gap and call it directional
why: Small groups swing widely; test the gap and report it as a lead.

q: Answers 51%, 47%, 32% and 25% add to 155%. That means...
why: It is a pick-several question, so each figure is not a share of one choice.

q: Doubling the sample size cuts the margin of error by about...
why: The margin shrinks with the square root of the sample, so about 30% for double.

q: The margin of error covers...
why: It covers chance from sampling, not bias in the questions or who replied.

q: Marginal P(X=x) is found by...
why: Sum the joint probabilities across all values of Y.

q: X and Y are independent when...
options: Each cell equals the product of its marginals
why: Zero covariance is weaker; independence needs every cell to match.

q: P(Y=1 and X=1)=0.5 and P(X=1)=0.7. P(Y=1 given X=1) is about...
why: 0.5 divided by 0.7.
